sources.title: NGSS 5-PS1-4: Conduct an investigation to determine whether the mixing of two or more substances results in new substances
OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 18.6 Occurrence, Preparation, and Properties of Carbonates (baking soda and acids)

note.text: Two glasses of water, each with the same spoonful of salt. Only the second one gets stirred.

steps.title: Water
steps.instruction: Draw the top of the water in each glass.

note.text: Water is the liquid the salt will mix into.

steps.title: Salt crystals
steps.instruction: Trace the salt crystals at the bottom of the first glass.

note.text: Just added, the salt sits at the bottom as tiny solid crystals you can see.

steps.title: Spoon
steps.instruction: Trace the spoon stirring the second glass.

note.text: Stirring helps the water break the crystals apart faster.

steps.title: Dissolved salt
steps.instruction: Dab the salt particles spread through the water.

note.text: The salt has dissolved: it split into particles too small to see, spread evenly through the water. They won't settle out.
note.remember: Dissolved = spread out, too small to see.

steps.title: Explain
steps.question: The salt in the stirred glass seems to disappear. Where did it go?

options.text: It broke into particles too small to see, spread through the water
options.feedback: Yes. The salt is still there. Its particles are mixed among the water's particles, too small to see.
Matter isn't destroyed. The salt split into tiny particles spread through the water.

options.text: It floated away into the air
options.feedback: Salt doesn't escape into the air. It's spread through the water in tiny particles.
It's still salt. Its particles are just mixed in among the water.

steps.title: New substance?
steps.question: Mixing baking soda with vinegar makes bubbles of a new gas. Does mixing salt into water make a new substance?

options.text: No, it's still salt and water, just mixed together
options.feedback: Right. Dissolving makes a mixture. Baking soda and an acid like vinegar react to make carbon dioxide gas, a new substance.
The salt only spread out into tiny particles. It's still salt mixed with water.
Salt in water doesn't fizz. That's baking soda and vinegar, which do make a new gas.

options.text: Every mixture makes a new substance
options.feedback: Some mixing does, like baking soda and vinegar. Salt and water just mix.

steps.title: Find the evidence
steps.question: You weigh salt and water, then mix them. How much will the salty water weigh?

options.text: The same as the salt and water together before
options.feedback: Yes. When substances mix, the total amount of matter stays the same. That's evidence the salt is still there.

options.text: Just as much as the water
options.feedback: The salt is still there, so it still counts. The total stays the same.
The salt only looks gone. The salty water weighs as much as both did before.
Mixing doesn't add matter. The total stays exactly the same.
